If you are staying in nearby bases such as Çalış Beach, Kayaköy, Faralya, Kabak Beach, or Üzümlü, the same road network is used for most access. A standard compact such as a Fiat Egea, Renault Clio, Hyundai i20, Citroen C3, Opel Astra, Skoda Scala, or Renault Taliant is enough for the main route, but a Dacia Duster or Fiat Egea Cross is more comfortable if you plan to visit Babadağ Mountain, Kelebekler Vadisi/Butterfly Valley, Gemiler Island, or the higher roads around Faralya. The standard car toll is 75 TL for the 2026 season, up from 60 TL in 2025, and the charge applies in both directions. The tunnel accepts cash, credit cards, and HGS, while the older mountain bypass is free, roughly 5.5 kilometres long, and known for 44 bends. The bypass is useful if you want a scenic route with views over the Göcek bays, but it can add 15–20 minutes in normal traffic. Rental companies do not always explain toll handling clearly, so ask whether HGS charges are billed later with an admin fee or preloaded into your invoice. The Göcek Tunnel — 75 TL Toll or 44-Bend Mountain Bypass Choose the fast tunnel or the scenic mountain road with views over Göcek bays HGS Electronic Tolls and Rental Billing Turkey uses HGS, or Hızlı Geçiş Sistemi, for electronic toll collection on highways and bridges, and OGS was retired in March 2022. Most Dalaman Airport vehicles have an HGS sticker on the windshield, so tolls are usually recorded automatically as you pass through the lane. That convenience matters on routes toward Fethiye, Kaş, and Pamukkale, where toll roads may appear on longer trips. The important point is billing transparency, because some suppliers charge the toll plus a service fee after return and others pre-authorise a toll credit at pickup. Ask the rental counter for a written HGS policy, and keep your contract because the official portal may require a Turkish ID number that most visitors do not have. Night Driving Tips: Dalaman to Fethiye Night driving between Dalaman and Fethiye requires slower speeds because large stretches of the D400 and nearby rural roads are unlit. Wildlife crossings are common in the surrounding Muğla Province, especially near wooded sections where wild boars, goats, cattle, and dogs may appear suddenly on the road. If your arrival is late, a Renault Symbol, Fiat Linea, or Kia Picanto is still suitable, but only if you drive conservatively and avoid overtaking on bends. Rain can make the asphalt slippery after long dry periods, because oil and dust collect on the surface and reduce grip when the first showers arrive. Yandex Navigasyon and Waze are useful for mobile speed-camera alerts, and the Turkish Traffic Police can be reached by dialling 155 in an emergency. Check our fuel stations and parking guide so you know where to refuel after a late arrival. For airport arrivals that finish after dark, a meet-and-greet or name sign pickup is often easier than trying to locate an off-airport desk in the terminal area. Road Construction Alert on the Fethiye–Ölüdeniz Corridor Road works on the 13.5-kilometre Fethiye–Ölüdeniz corridor are important for 2026 travellers because the project is backed by a 328-million-TL budget and staged traffic management. Stage 1 between Patlangıç and Ovacık has been completed with widening to 15 metres, Stage 2 between Ovacık and the city center is in progress, Stage 3 between Hisarönü and Ölüdeniz has been completed, and Stage 4 between Ölüdeniz and Kayaköy is mostly completed. Construction is usually paused from June to August, which means April–May and September–October are the most likely months for delays, diversions, or single-lane sections. If you are staying in Fethiye, Ölüdeniz, Kayaköy, or Ovacık during those shoulder months, allow extra time and expect variable speeds near work zones. article.description: Car rental FAQ for Ölüdeniz: DLM Airport is 60 km away, Blue Lagoon parking costs up to 650 TL, Göcek Tunnel toll is 75 TL, and fuel is available in Ovacık and Fethiye.
article.body: Do I actually need to rent a car in Ölüdeniz? A car is useful for regional sightseeing in Ölüdeniz, but a car is not necessary if you only want beach days and short local transfers. The dolmuş between Ölüdeniz and Fethiye runs about every 10 minutes and costs 25–35 TL per passenger, while Blue Lagoon parking can cost 500–650 TL for car entry in peak season. For day trips to Saklıkent Gorge, Patara Beach, Kayaköy, Tlos, Pinara, Xanthos, Letoon, Faralya, Kabak Beach, Butterfly Valley (Kelebekler Vadisi), and Gemiler Island, a rental car saves time on the Lycian Coast and the Turquoise Coast. How far is Dalaman Airport from Ölüdeniz? Dalaman Airport (DLM) is 60 km from Ölüdeniz and the drive usually takes 75–90 minutes via the D400 highway or the Göcek Tunnel route. Rental counters are typically in the airport terminal, and many providers use a meet-and-greet service in the arrivals hall with a name sign for handover. The Göcek Tunnel toll is 75 TL per vehicle in 2026, while the older mountain road is free but usually adds 15–20 minutes. Can I use a debit card for the rental deposit? Major international brands usually require an embossed credit card for the preauthorisation deposit, not a debit card. Enterprise, Avis, Europcar, Sixt, Budget, and Garenta commonly block debit-card holds, while local firms such as Cizgi Rent a Car, Babadan Rent a Car, Oscar Rent a Car, Yelken Rent a Car, Marin Rent a Car, Turunç Rent a Car, TinyAkropol, Circular Car Hire, and Apple Rent a Car may accept a debit card or cash deposit depending on the branch. Under Turkish rental practice, the deposit is separate from the rental payment, and some local companies still accept cash even though the June 2017 cash-payment rule applies to the rental itself. Do I need an international driving permit for Turkey? A standard national driving licence is sufficient for short tourist rentals in Turkey for up to 90 days. Drivers from the EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia, and many other countries are typically accepted, and the minimum rental age is often 19–21 depending on the supplier. If you plan to stay and drive in Turkey for more than 90 consecutive days, an International Driving Permit may become necessary, so check the rental policy before you collect the car. Is a standard car enough or do I need a 4WD/SUV? A standard economy car is enough for most paved routes around Ölüdeniz, including the D400 highway, Fethiye, Ölüdeniz, Ovacık, Hisarönü, Çalış Beach, Göcek, Dalyan, Köyceğiz, Üzümlü, and the road toward Kaş and Kalkan. Common fleet choices in the area include Fiat Egea, Fiat Egea Cross, Fiat Linea, Renault Clio, Renault Symbol, Renault Taliant, Hyundai i20, Hyundai Bayon, Citroen C3, Opel Astra, Skoda Scala, Ford Focus, Kia Picanto, Nissan Qashqai, Dacia Duster, Dacia Lodgy, Volkswagen Passat, Toyota Hilux, and Suzuki Samurai. A 4WD is mainly useful for rougher access roads near Kabak Beach or mountain tracks around Babadağ Mountain, and some contracts exclude unpaved-road damage from CDW, SCDW, FDW, or zero excess cover. What does "Kasko" mean on my rental contract? "Kasko" is the Turkish term often used for collision and damage cover, and it is usually linked to CDW, SCDW, or full coverage wording on rental contracts. Standard Kasko normally includes an excess/deductible, also called franchise or muafiyet, while zero excess products remove the driver’s liability for many damage claims. In Turkey, renters may also see Zorunlu Trafik Sigortası or ZMSS for mandatory third-party liability, but that policy does not replace rental damage protection for the vehicle itself. Where can I get fuel near Ölüdeniz? There are no fuel stations inside the Ölüdeniz resort area, so drivers usually refuel in Ovacık or Fethiye before returning to the beach zone. Ovacık is about 4–5 km away and Fethiye center is about 14 km away, where major brands such as Shell, Opet, and Petrol Ofisi operate on the Muğla Province road network. As of March 2026, fuel prices were listed at 64.62 TL per litre for petrol and 77.90 TL per litre for diesel, so a full tank is the safest option before a long coastal drive. What should I watch out for with parking? Blue Lagoon parking is limited and can fill before 11:00 AM in peak season, so early arrival is the best way to avoid queueing. A common backup is free street parking near the Ölüdeniz Mosque, followed by a 15-minute walk, while Fethiye market day on Tuesday usually creates heavier traffic in the town center. faqs.q: Do I need full coverage for a rental car in Ölüdeniz?
faqs.a: Yes, full coverage is the safest option for most travelers because it can reduce the deductible to zero and protect against common damage items. A typical CDW quote might leave you with a €500–€900 excess, while SCDW or FDW can add €8–€20/day and reduce the hold on your card. Caveat: full coverage does not always include off-road damage, wrong fuel, lost keys, or deliberate negligence, so the contract still matters.

faqs.q: Can I pick up a rental car directly at Dalaman Airport (DLM)?
faqs.a: Yes, many suppliers offer terminal pickup, arrivals hall counters, or meet-and-greet handover at Dalaman Airport (DLM). Brands like Avis, Europcar, Sixt, Enterprise, Budget, and Garenta often have a staffed desk or a shuttle to the rental counter, while some local companies use a name sign outside the terminal. Caveat: the exact handover point and shuttle time should be confirmed before landing because smaller suppliers may operate only during daylight hours.

faqs.q: Is insurance included in the rental price in Turkey?
faqs.a: Yes, ZMSS third-party liability is mandatory, but CDW, SCDW, FDW, and zero excess are not always included in the headline price. A low quote for a Renault Clio or Fiat Egea may cover only the legal minimum, while full coverage usually costs more per day but lowers the deductible and deposit hold. Caveat: always check whether the booking page names Kasko, muafiyet, and the exclusions list before you pay.

faqs.q: What is the safest car for Fethiye and Ölüdeniz roads?

Stage 2: Tlos to Saklıkent Gorge: The next 8 km take you to Saklıkent Gorge, where the road passes pine forest and riverside restaurants; in peak season, arriving before 10:30 helps avoid queues. See our attraction parking guide for lot details and payment tips. Best vehicle choice: A compact model such as a Renault Clio, Hyundai i20, or Kia Picanto is easier than a larger SUV on the tight bends and passing points. This is especially useful on the return climb when traffic meets descending vehicles near the olive groves. Parking and boat access: Beach attendants at Gemiler Bay usually charge about 10 TL in summer and often no fee in the off-season, while boats run from the beach to Gemiler Island, also known as St. Nicholas Island. The island entrance fee was approximately 70–100 TL as of the 2025–2026 season, so budget accordingly for the day. Main route and drive time: The standard route is Ölüdeniz → Fethiye → D400 → Kalkan → Kaş, covering about 110 km in roughly 2 hours without stops. This corridor is suitable for nearly all standard rentals, including Fiat Egea Cross, Dacia Duster, Ford Focus, Volkswagen Passat, and Nissan Qashqai. Letoon: Letoon sits just off the D400 and works well as a short detour if you want a quieter archaeological stop before continuing to Kalkan or Kaş. The site is also a useful trail access point for walkers heading toward the Lycian Way. The D400 is a national road with frequent upgrades, but evening traffic near Kalkan and Kaş can slow in summer, so build in extra time if you are connecting this drive with a ferry, dinner reservation, or hotel check-in. Üzümlü (Yeşilüzümlü): Üzümlü sits on a plateau over 600 m above sea level and is usually reached in 25–30 minutes from Fethiye, about 15–17 km away. The access road is wide and well maintained, making it easy in a small car like a Fiat Egea, Hyundai i20, or Renault Symbol, and the village is a practical lunch stop when coastal temperatures reach 40°C. Fethiye to Dalyan: Dalyan is about 61 km from Fethiye and usually takes 50–75 minutes via the D400 through Ortaca, with a scenic extension through Köyceğiz adding 20–30 minutes. Along the way, Göcek is a worthwhile marina stop, while Dalyan itself offers the rock tombs, İztuzu Beach, and the Sultaniye hot springs. Nearby destinations: For longer coastal loops, travelers often combine Dalyan with Köyceğiz or a return route past Fethiye, while others use the same area as a staging point for Kaş, Kalkan, or Pamukkale on multi-day trips. These are all paved road options, so they remain suitable for standard hire cars. 4WD vs Standard Car — What You Actually Need For most scenic drives around Ölüdeniz, a standard car is enough, and a 4WD is only necessary for specific unpaved sections. Ask for the deposit amount, the excess amount, and the road-use exclusions in writing at Dalaman Airport (DLM) before driving away. If you plan to stay within the paved network around Ölüdeniz, a small hatchback usually offers the best value. Frequently Asked Questions Ready to explore the Lycian Coast? Tlos–Saklıkent–Pinara Ancient Cities Loop The Tlos–Saklıkent–Pinara loop is the best full-day cultural drive from Ölüdeniz, combining the D400 highway, mountain roads, and three major Lycian sites in one route. Route, distance, and timing: The loop is roughly 120–140 km round trip from Ölüdeniz and usually takes 3–3.5 hours of driving time, with a realistic full-day schedule from about 09:30 to 18:30. The route works well in a compact rental such as a Fiat Linea, Renault Taliant, Opel Astra, or Skoda Scala. Stage 1: Ölüdeniz to Tlos: Drive via Fethiye and join the D400 highway, then follow signs for Tlos after about 22 km; the final 10 km to the site are on a narrow but paved road, and parking is free by the entrance area. Tlos is one of the most important Lycian settlements, and the site works well as a first stop because the approach is straightforward for standard cars. Stage 2: Tlos to Saklıkent Gorge: The next 8 km take you to Saklıkent Gorge, where the road passes pine forest and riverside restaurants; in peak season, arriving before 10:30 helps avoid queues. Entry is typically 100–120 TL per person, and the area is a common stop on guided Jeep Safari tours as well as independent self-drives. See our attraction parking guide for lot details and payment tips. Stage 3: Saklıkent to Pinara: The final leg heads back toward the main highway, with Pinara reached by a short turnoff near Minare village; recent roadworks have improved the approach from gravel to paved surface. Pinara is a strong fit for travelers who want a quieter site than Xanthos or Patara Beach, and a simple sedan like a Renault Clio or Citroen C3 is enough for the access road. Turkish road conditions change after winter maintenance and municipal works, so verify any local roadworks notice and keep to paved sections if your contract includes a mileage cap or off-road exclusion. The Lycian Coast Awaits From Butterfly Valley to Kabak Beach — Ölüdeniz’s most dramatic coastal drives Kayaköy to Gemiler Island The Kayaköy to Gemiler Island drive is the easiest half-day trip from Ölüdeniz, combining the ghost village of Kayaköy with the sea access at Gemiler Bay and Gemiler Island. Route and drive time: From Hisarönü above Ölüdeniz, the road to Kayaköy takes about 10 minutes, and roadside parking is usually free; the village entry fee is around 100 TL and opening hours are typically 08:30–18:30. From Kayaköy, follow signs for Gemiler Adası through Kınalı village to the beach road, which is paved all the way but very narrow on the final descent. Best vehicle choice: A compact model such as a Renault Clio, Hyundai i20, or Kia Picanto is easier than a larger SUV on the tight bends and passing points. This is especially useful on the return climb when traffic meets descending vehicles near the olive groves. Parking and boat access: Beach attendants at Gemiler Bay usually charge about 10 TL in summer and often no fee in the off-season, while boats run from the beach to Gemiler Island, also known as St. Nicholas Island. The island entrance fee was approximately 70–100 TL as of the 2025–2026 season, so budget accordingly for the day. The D400 Coastal Route to Kaş, Kalkan, Xanthos, and Patara The D400 highway is the core coastal route of the Turkish Aegean and Turquoise Coast, and the Ölüdeniz to Kaş drive is one of the strongest one-day scenic runs in Muğla Province. Main route and drive time: The standard route is Ölüdeniz → Fethiye → D400 → Kalkan → Kaş, covering about 110 km in roughly 2 hours without stops. This corridor is suitable for nearly all standard rentals, including Fiat Egea Cross, Dacia Duster, Ford Focus, Volkswagen Passat, and Nissan Qashqai. If you are picking up at the airport, our Dalaman Airport pickup guide covers the handover process. If Kalkan is your base for the Turquoise Coast rather than a day stop, the local guide to renting a car in Kalkan covers in-town pickup points and parking. Xanthos: Around the 65 km mark, Xanthos offers a UNESCO-listed ancient capital with easy roadside parking and minimal walking from the vehicle. For travelers interested in Lycian history, Xanthos is one of the clearest cultural stops on the route. Patara Beach and ancient city: The Patara turnoff comes around the 70 km point, and the beach stretches for about 18 km with a seasonal closing time of 20:00 for Caretta caretta nesting protection. Expect dual pricing for the combined site, with foreign visitor entry around €15, and note that parking is on a boardwalk about 100–200 m from the sea. Letoon: Letoon sits just off the D400 and works well as a short detour if you want a quieter archaeological stop before continuing to Kalkan or Kaş. The site is also a useful trail access point for walkers heading toward the Lycian Way. The D400 is a national road with frequent upgrades, but evening traffic near Kalkan and Kaş can slow in summer, so build in extra time if you are connecting this drive with a ferry, dinner reservation, or hotel check-in. Lycian Heritage by Car Tlos, Saklıkent, Pinara, Xanthos, and Patara — all reachable in a standard rental Mountain Village Escapes Mountain villages near Ölüdeniz offer cooler air, shorter drives, and a different side of Fethiye and Muğla Province away from the coast. Üzümlü (Yeşilüzümlü): Üzümlü sits on a plateau over 600 m above sea level and is usually reached in 25–30 minutes from Fethiye, about 15–17 km away. The access road is wide and well maintained, making it easy in a small car like a Fiat Egea, Hyundai i20, or Renault Symbol, and the village is a practical lunch stop when coastal temperatures reach 40°C. Fethiye to Dalyan: Dalyan is about 61 km from Fethiye and usually takes 50–75 minutes via the D400 through Ortaca, with a scenic extension through Köyceğiz adding 20–30 minutes. Along the way, Göcek is a worthwhile marina stop, while Dalyan itself offers the rock tombs, İztuzu Beach, and the Sultaniye hot springs. Nearby destinations: For longer coastal loops, travelers often combine Dalyan with Köyceğiz or a return route past Fethiye, while others use the same area as a staging point for Kaş, Kalkan, or Pamukkale on multi-day trips. These are all paved road options, so they remain suitable for standard hire cars. 4WD vs Standard Car — What You Actually Need For most scenic drives around Ölüdeniz, a standard car is enough, and a 4WD is only necessary for specific unpaved sections. faqs.q: Is a 4WD needed for the Kabak Coast Road?
faqs.a: No, a 4WD is only needed for the final descent from Kabak village to Kabak Beach. The paved road to Kabak village is about 14 km from Ölüdeniz and is routinely driven by standard rentals such as Fiat Egea and Renault Clio. The exception is the steep unpaved beach track, which can fall outside CDW, SCDW, and Kasko coverage.

faqs.q: Can I drive from Ölüdeniz to Patara Beach in a normal rental car?
faqs.a: Yes, the Ölüdeniz to Patara Beach route is fully manageable in a standard rental car. The drive uses the D400 and is about 110 km in total if combined with Kalkan and Kaş, while the Patara turnoff and parking area are designed for normal road cars. article.headline: Traffic Fines in a Rental Car Around Ölüdeniz: Who Actually Pays, and How Much
article.description: Got a fine in an Ölüdeniz hire car? Since February 2026 it is issued to you, not the rental firm. What each company adds on top, and why you cannot pay it yourself.
article.articleBody: Last verified: 2 August 2026 The short answer. Since 27 February 2026 the notice goes to the renter, not the rental firm — but you still cannot settle it yourself, so the firm pays it and bills your card with its own fee attached. Cizgi adds a flat 300 TL per fine — the only structure here that leaves you below the headline figure on a large fine. Oscar adds 25% of the base fine, which almost exactly cancels the state's 25% early-payment discount: you pay roughly the full base fine. Garenta adds 30% (plus 12% on HGS tolls), so you pay more than the base fine — a 5,000 TL red light costs you 5,250 TL. The 25% discount runs one month from notification, and whether it reaches you depends on how fast your firm pays. If you hired a car in Ölüdeniz and a fine has landed — or you're worried one might — here is the plain answer. Since 27 February 2026, a new law (No. 7574, amending Highway Traffic Law No. 2918) means the penalty for an offence committed in a hire car is now normally issued to you, the renter, not the rental company, once police confirm through KABİS (Kiralık Araç Bildirim Sistemi, the rental notification system) that the car was on hire that day. In practice, you almost certainly cannot rely on paying it yourself through a Turkish government payment channel — those channels are built around Turkish citizens and Turkish-registered companies, not tourists. What actually happens is that the rental firm settles the fine and then charges your card, adding its own handling fee on top. Below is that combined figure — the fine plus the firm's fee — worked through for the most common offences, and an explanation of why the portal advice you'll find on forums does not apply to a Turkish-plated hire car. Before 27 February 2026, a speed camera that caught a hire car's plate produced a penalty notice addressed to the registered owner — the rental company — under Article 116 of the Highway Traffic Law (KTK, Law No. 2918). The company then had internal terms to pass the cost to whoever had the car booked. Law No. 7574, passed by parliament on 12 February 2026 and published in the Resmî Gazete on 27 February 2026, changes that starting point: where KABİS confirms the vehicle was under an active rental contract on the date of the offence, the notice is directed to the renter instead. The law took effect on publication. What no official source spells out is the mechanics for a foreign tourist with no Turkish address and no T.C. Kimlik number — there is simply no published procedure for serving a notice on someone who isn't reachable inside the Turkish administrative system. In practice, that gap is filled by the rental contract you signed: the company remains the party that actually clears the debt with the traffic authority and then recharges your card or deposit. If a fine reaches you, ask the firm for a copy of the penalty record (ceza tutanağı) and the date of the offence, so you can at least check it falls inside your rental period. Where a notice is served on the rental company rather than the renter, it goes through e-Tebligat, the electronic notification system, and is legally deemed served at the end of the fifth day after it lands in the company's electronic inbox. That five-day clock is what starts the countdown to the 25% early-payment discount described below. Either way, the contractual route to your money is the same one you signed at the pick-up desk: a clause allowing the firm to charge fines, tolls and associated fees to the card on file, sometimes weeks or months after you've flown home from Dalaman. This is standard across Turkish rental agreements and is exactly why a charge can appear with no warning — the underlying offence, the notice, and the firm's own payment cycle can each take weeks. For the full rundown of what else can legitimately hit your card under a Turkish rental contract, see our rental insurance and scam-avoidance guide. This table sets out the 2026 base fine, the discounted price if it's paid promptly, and what each named rental firm's published fee structure adds — calculated, as documented, on the base fine rather than the discounted amount actually paid. Offence (2026 rate) — Base fine — Paid within 1 month (25% off) — + Cizgi Rent a Car (flat 300 TL) — + Garenta (30% of base fine) — + Oscar Rent a Car (25% of base fine) Speeding, 10–30% over limit — 2,719 TL — 2,039 TL — 2,339 TL — 2,855 TL — 2,719 TL Speeding, 30–50% over limit — 5,662 TL — 4,247 TL — 4,547 TL — 5,945 TL — 5,662 TL Speeding, more than 50% over — 11,631 TL — 8,723 TL — 9,023 TL — 12,213 TL — 11,631 TL Running a red light — 5,000 TL — 3,750 TL — 4,050 TL — 5,250 TL — 5,000 TL Illegal or incorrect parking — 1,246 TL — 935 TL — 1,235 TL — 1,308 TL — 1,246 TL Driving the wrong way — 25,000 TL — 18,750 TL — 19,050 TL — 26,250 TL — 25,000 TL The pattern is worth reading carefully, because it isn't intuitive. At Oscar's 25% fee (calculated on the base fine), the fee is almost exactly the same size as the 25% discount the state gives for early payment — so the two cancel out and you end up paying close to the full, undiscounted base fine. At Garenta's 30%, the fee is larger than the discount, so you end up paying more than the base fine — the government's early-payment saving never reaches you at all; the firm keeps it and adds its own margin besides. Cizgi's flat 300 TL is the only structure here where you land below the headline base figure once the discount is banked. This is the documented basis for how these three firms describe their fees, not a guarantee — a firm could in principle calculate its percentage on the discounted amount instead, which would produce lower totals than shown here. Two firms sit outside this table on other terms. Garenta also charges 12% on HGS toll usage specifically (separate from its 30% fine fee — see the tolls section below). Avis Türkiye and Budget Türkiye use a variable model: the discounted fine plus a fixed service fee, but neither publishes the fixed amount, so it cannot be calculated here. The Fethiye-based local operators — Babadan, Yelken, Marin, TinyAkropol, Circular and Apple — do not publish a fine-handling fee at all. Ask for the figure in writing before you sign. For the full catalogue of Turkish fine categories beyond these six, see our rental insurance and scam-avoidance guide. No — not on a Turkish-plated hire car, and the portal everyone recommends is the wrong one. The advice that circulates on expat forums — "just pay it on the GİB portal" — does not apply to your situation, and it's worth explaining why clearly. The dijital.gib.gov.tr "Yabancı Plakalı Araç Ödemeleri" (Foreign-Plated Vehicle Payments) portal is ring-fenced for exactly what its name says: vehicles carrying foreign number plates, typically someone who drove their own car across the border into Türkiye. A car hired from a desk at Dalaman carries a Turkish plate, so this portal simply does not recognise it, regardless of your own nationality. The deeper reason is structural: Turkish-plated vehicles are linked in the tax system to the registered owner's T.C. Kimlik number (for an individual) or VKN, the corporate tax number (for a company — in this case, the rental firm). A tourist holds neither, so GİB İnteraktif and e-Devlet will ask for credentials a visitor doesn't have. That said, it is occasionally reported that a PTT counter or a bank branch will accept a payment against a Turkish-plated fine if you present the penalty record number and the vehicle's plate — but this is not documented as a reliable or guaranteed route, and it is not something to plan around. The rental company, holding the VKN the system recognises, remains the party you should expect to actually settle the debt. Discount window: 25% off if paid within one month of notification — extended from the previous 15-day window by an amendment published on 31 January 2024. The month runs from notification, not from the offence; where the notice reaches the rental company via e-Tebligat, the clock starts on the fifth day after delivery. Interest: 5% per month under KTK Article 115, with any part-month counted as a full month. Ceiling: disputed — the prevailing reading caps the interest at twice the fine (a three-times total), while other readings cap the total debt itself. Miss the window and the fine reverts to its full amount, then starts accruing that interest. For a renter the ceiling dispute is largely academic, because the rental company normally settles long before any ceiling would bite. The practical point is simpler: a well-organised firm pays fast and avoids interest altogether; a slow one lets the window close and adds accruing interest to whatever it then bills you. The governing text is Highway Traffic Law No. 2918, as amended by Law No. 7574 in the Resmî Gazete of 27 February 2026. Turkish motorway and bridge tolls run on HGS, a separate system with its own escalation, unconnected to KTK penalty fines: Days since the toll passage — What's actually owed Days 1–15 — Base toll only — no penalty Days 16–45 — Base toll + 1× the toll amount (you pay double) After day 45 — Base toll + 4× the toll amount (five times the original toll in total) The HGS sticker on a hire car is registered to the rental company's own corporate account, not yours. If the firm lets that account's balance run dry, the multiplier above is generated automatically on their side — and it's routinely passed straight to the renter's card, often appearing only as a vague "HGS usage fee" line with no breakdown. Garenta specifically charges 12% on top of HGS toll usage. If you're driving in from Dalaman and crossing any tolled sections en route, our Dalaman Airport pickup and HGS tolls guide covers what to check with the desk before you leave the lot. An illegally parked hire car in the Fethiye area that gets towed is taken to Ecesu Oto Kurtarma – Oto Park ve İcra Deposu, on the D400 bypass in the Çamköy neighbourhood. Muğla is classified as a "2nd Region" zone under the 2026 official trustee (yediemin) tariff, which sets: Component — 2026 Muğla (2nd Region) rate Recovery / hook-up base fee — 735 TL Per kilometre towed — 73.40–98 TL per km Storage — 110.10 TL per day These release costs are paid in cash directly at the pound to get your car back — they are separate from, and additional to, the underlying illegal-parking fine (1,246 TL, or 935 TL at the 25% discount), which still reaches you later through the rental company by the route described above. For everyday parking that doesn't end in a tow, see our parking and fuel guide. Enforcement in the area is concentrated on two stretches of road. The D400 through Fethiye steps down in stages — from 110 km/h out on the open road to 70, then 50 km/h through the built-up section around the Çamköy and Günlükbaşı junctions — and is monitored by fixed EDS (Electronic Supervision System) cameras. Exact camera positions aren't published anywhere reliable, so treat the whole urban stretch as monitored rather than trying to spot the equipment. The mountain road linking Fethiye to Ölüdeniz via Ovacık and Hisarönü carries a 50 km/h limit for good reason: steep gradients, tight switchbacks and heavy pedestrian traffic in season. Enforcement there in high season combines fixed radar with mobile Jandarma checkpoints. A new bypass road toward Kıdrak, intended to ease the Kumburnu bottleneck, began construction in April 2026 with a target completion of June 2026 — check locally whether it's open to traffic before relying on it as a shortcut. Road segment — Speed limit — Enforcement D400, open road outside Fethiye — 110 km/h — Fixed EDS cameras along the corridor D400 approaching Fethiye — 70 km/h — Step-down zone before the built-up section D400 through Çamköy and Günlükbaşı — 50 km/h — Built-up section, fixed EDS Fethiye – Ölüdeniz via Ovacık and Hisarönü — 50 km/h — Fixed radar plus mobile Jandarma checkpoints in season Yes, but the practical route is narrow for a tourist. You have 15 days from the date of notification to file an objection with the Sulh Ceza Hâkimliği (Criminal Court of Peace) covering the location of the offence. There's no filing fee, though court costs can follow if the objection is rejected. Filing online through UYAP or e-Devlet requires a Turkish qualified electronic signature or a registered mobile signature — neither of which a visiting tourist holds — so in practice your realistic options are filing in person before you leave the country, or granting power of attorney to a Turkish lawyer, which usually costs more than the fine itself. One point worth knowing before you decide: paying at the 25% discounted rate does not waive your right to appeal — if the appeal later succeeds, the money is refunded. Do I have to pay a traffic fine from my Ölüdeniz rental car myself? No. Since the 27 February 2026 change (Law No. 7574), the notice may be addressed to you as the renter once KABİS confirms the rental, but the actual government payment channels are not built for foreign tourists — no source describes a reliable procedure for a renter with no Turkish ID to settle it directly. In practice the rental company pays it and recharges your card. Can I use the GİB "Yabancı Plakalı Araç" portal to pay it myself? No. That portal is for vehicles on foreign number plates. A car hired at Dalaman carries a Turkish plate, so the portal doesn't recognise it, and the underlying tax-system link (T.C. Kimlik / VKN) doesn't match a tourist anyway. How much extra will the rental company charge on top of the fine? It depends entirely on the firm. Cizgi Rent a Car charges a flat 300 TL per fine. Garenta charges 30% of the base fine (plus 12% on HGS toll usage separately). Oscar Rent a Car charges 25% of the base fine — which, worked through the numbers, roughly cancels the government's 25% early-payment discount. Avis Türkiye and Budget Türkiye use the discounted fine plus an unpublished fixed service fee. Local Fethiye firms don't publish a figure at all — ask before you sign. Will I still get the benefit of the 25% early-payment discount? It depends on the firm, and the two documented practices point in different directions. Some rental companies pay within the one-month window, bank the 25% saving, and bill the renter only the discounted amount. Others are reported to keep the saving for themselves and bill the renter the full, undiscounted fine regardless of when they paid. There's no way to tell in advance which practice applies to your booking, so it's worth asking directly. Can I be stopped from leaving Türkiye over an unpaid fine? No exit ban applies to a tourist leaving on a Turkish-plated hire car with an unpaid fine — that strict rule is for foreign-plated vehicles. Turkish legal sources do indicate an unpaid fine can potentially be collected on your next entry to the country, though sources aren't unanimous on this, so treat it as a real but not certain risk worth clearing rather than something to panic about. Is it worth appealing a fine? Only if you're confident the offence is wrong and you're willing to either file in person at the Sulh Ceza Hâkimliği before leaving Türkiye, or pay a Turkish lawyer with power of attorney — which usually costs more than the fine. Paying the discounted amount first doesn't forfeit that right; a successful appeal gets the money refunded. Are HGS toll charges handled the same way as fines? No. HGS escalates on its own schedule: no penalty for the first 15 days, double the toll from day 16–45, and after day 45, the base toll plus four times the toll — five times the original amount in total. It's tied to the rental firm's own HGS account balance, not a KABİS-linked penalty notice, and is often billed to renters simply as an "HGS usage fee."

faqs.a: No. HGS escalates on its own schedule: no penalty for the first 15 days, double the toll from day 16–45, and after day 45, the base toll plus four times the toll — five times the original amount in total. It's tied to the rental firm's own HGS account balance, not a KABİS-linked penalty notice, and is often billed to renters simply as an "HGS usage fee."
